segments.contextBefore: When working with Wi-Fi, your best option for recording a packet trace depends on whether you’re interested in the network traffic itself, or in the details of how the Wi-Fi network manages traffic.
segments.contextAfter: If you’re primarily interested in the traffic going over the Wi-Fi — that is, you would like to ignore all the low-level details of Wi-Fi and treat the Wi-Fi network like an Ethernet network without all those pesky wires — use one of the following high-level approaches:

segments.contextAfter: If possible, run the packet trace on one of the machines involved in the communication — including using RVI to record an iOS packet trace. That’s the easiest solution. See [`Recording a Packet Trace`](recording-a-packet-trace.md) for instructions.

segments.contextAfter: If your Wi-Fi access point supports bridge mode (notably, all Apple base stations do), you can bridge the Wi-Fi network on to an Ethernet network and then use standard Ethernet techniques to capture a packet trace. You won’t be able to see Wi-Fi to Wi-Fi traffic, but in many situations that’s not a problem.

segments.contextAfter: If you enable Internet Sharing on your Mac, and have your Wi-Fi clients join the shared network, you can run your packet trace program on the Mac and see all the Wi-Fi traffic. If you target the Mac’s Wi-Fi interface, you will see all traffic, including Wi-Fi to Wi-Fi traffic. If you target the Mac’s Ethernet interface, you will only see traffic entering or leaving the Wi-Fi network.
